brief: Nomura's Charlie McElligott argues Monday's 84%-advancing S&P rally was driven mechanically by a vol crush, not demand. Dealers had gone short puts and OTM puts after Thursday's record CBOE put volume. As spot rose and implied vol collapsed, those puts lost delta twice, forcing dealers to buy back short futures hedges (vanna), while rallying calls neared ITM and added more buying. The VIX fell from 28 to 20 in roughly two and a half sessions. On Tuesday, that vol meltdown stalled, so the rally stalled too, just as October CPI printed hot (0.4% month-over-month, core 0.3% versus 0.2% expected), pushing December 50bp-hike odds to 14% after Fed Governor Waller had floated that condition in a Monday speech. McElligott flags record options volumes, leveraged-ETF rebalancing, and reduced vol-control-fund equity allocation as a powder keg of two-way moves, and notes VVIX realized volatility at a record high, above the 2018 Volmageddon episode. He expects a wider distribution of outcomes and a structurally higher VIX floor, tied to AI capex doubts feeding through to nominal GDP, equity vol, skew, correlation, rates, and credit.
